issues.legal_issue: The nature and use of property on the date of transfer are relevant to its valuation for stamp duty, while a later change in use is not.
material_facts: The property was used for residential purposes when the sale deed was executed, and the purchasers said they had paid stamp duty on that basis.
The authorities assessed the property at a higher value after inspection, including on the basis of its area and building details.
The property was used for commercial purposes at a later point, but its residential use on the transfer date was not seriously disputed.
issues.conclusion: The property’s nature and use on the date of purchase were relevant to stamp-duty valuation; its later commercial use was not. The Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s order quashing the demand and penalty.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 47A and 33 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, stamp-duty valuation concerns the property as it stood at the time of the transfer. The Court held that the nature of user is relatable to the date of purchase and that later commercial use is not a relevant criterion for that valuation. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.stamp_duty_valuation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the assessment of stamp duty on a transfer of property.
predicates.property_used_residential_at_transfer: The property was used for residential purposes when the transfer took place.
predicates.commercial_use_started_later: The property came to be used for commercial purposes after the transfer.

issues.definition: When a stamp-duty valuation proceeding concerns property used residentially at transfer but commercially later, the assessment uses the property’s user at transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge under writ jurisdiction is not rejected on the basis of an available statutory appeal when the opposing government did not seriously raise that objection before the High Court.
material_facts: The purchasers challenged the administrative stamp-duty order and demand by filing a writ petition.
A statutory appeal was available under the applicable law.
The government did not seriously object before the High Court to the writ petition proceeding without use of that alternative remedy.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the government’s alternative-remedy objection at that stage, while observing that it was relevant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the availability of an appeal under the Act and the High Court’s jurisdiction under Article 226. It did not treat the availability of an alternative remedy as a ground to reject the challenge in this appeal because the government had not seriously raised the objection before the High Court. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_administrative_order: A person challenged an administrative order by filing a writ petition.
predicates.statutory_appeal_available: The applicable law provided an appeal against the administrative order.
predicates.government_did_not_press_alternative_rem: The government opposing the writ petition did not seriously raise the availability of an appeal before the High Court.

issues.definition: When an administrative order is challenged by writ despite an available appeal, the alternative-remedy objection is not entertained if the opposing government did not seriously raise it before the High Court.
